practice: What is an activity transition in a preschool programme?
The change from one activity or routine to another, such as moving from outdoor play to handwashing.
What is a learning corner?
An accessible area organised for a particular kind of exploration, such as books, construction or pretend play.
What is a contingency plan for an outdoor session?
An alternative arrangement that preserves learning and safety when conditions such as heavy rain prevent the planned session.
Give one example of a locally available learning material.
Clean, large, smooth leaves for supervised sorting and comparison.
What is meant by child choice in programme planning?
Providing meaningful opportunities for children to select activities, materials or ways of participating within safe limits.
Name one purpose of a visual daily schedule.
It helps children anticipate what will happen next and understand changes in the routine.
What is a resource inventory in an ECCE centre?
A record of available materials, their condition and any repair or replacement needs.
What is a quiet area used for in an early childhood classroom?
It offers a comfortable supervised place for rest, looking at books or settling when a child needs less stimulation.
Give one example of a transition cue.
A familiar short song that signals it is time to put materials away.
What does flexible grouping mean?
Changing group size or membership according to the activity and children's needs rather than keeping fixed ability groups.
Why should a daily schedule alternate active and quieter experiences?
Children need opportunities for movement as well as rest and concentration.
Alternation can reduce fatigue and help children re-engage without expecting prolonged sitting.
Why should materials be placed on accessible shelves?
Children can make choices, obtain materials and practise returning them with suitable support.
Accessible organisation also helps children with different physical needs participate more independently.
Suggest two ways to avoid long waiting lines during routines.
Use small staggered groups for tasks such as handwashing.
Provide a simple supervised activity for children waiting for their turn rather than requiring prolonged inactivity.
How can a teacher plan for a new child's first week?
Arrange a welcoming, predictable routine and learn about the child's familiar language and comfort needs.
Allow gradual participation and communicate with the family about the child's adjustment.
Why should a classroom plan include clear movement routes?
Clear routes reduce collisions and improve access to materials and exits.
They also support independent movement, including for children using mobility aids.
How can a centre include a family unable to attend daytime meetings?
Offer a feasible alternative, such as a brief agreed telephone conversation or another meeting time.
Share essential information in an accessible language and invite the family's observations without treating absence as lack of interest.
Suggest two ways to make a book corner inviting.
Provide a comfortable accessible space with books displayed so children can see and choose them.
Include varied, familiar and multilingual books that reflect children's lives and interests.
Why should the teacher review an activity immediately after conducting it?
Fresh observations help identify what engaged children and what limited participation.
They guide changes in materials, timing or support for the next session.
How can children's interests inform a planned theme?
Listen to their questions and notice recurring interests during play.
Use these observations to select meaningful experiences while retaining developmental goals and room for new exploration.
What should a teacher check before inviting a community visitor?
Check the visitor's suitability, the purpose and the accessibility of the activity.
Explain safeguarding arrangements and ensure children remain under the centre's supervision.
Suggest three improvements to a classroom where construction play disrupts quiet reading.
Separate the construction and reading areas using safe furniture arrangements while maintaining supervision.
Provide enough space and suitable surfaces for building so movement and noise are contained as far as practical.
Review the arrangement with children and adjust it through observation instead of simply prohibiting active play.
How can a routine support independence without rushing children?
Break the routine into understandable steps and model them clearly.
Place suitable materials within reach and allow children time to attempt the steps with help when needed.
Notice progress and adapt support rather than complete every task for the child or punish slower participation.
How would you adapt a planned nature walk during heavy rain?
Move to a safe indoor observation point or use previously collected safe natural materials.
Retain the purpose through comparing leaves, listening to rain or discussing observed changes.
Reschedule outdoor exploration when safe and explain the change using a familiar schedule cue.
Give three considerations when selecting a classroom theme.
Choose a context meaningful to children's experiences while avoiding stereotypes or assumptions that all families live alike.
Check that it offers varied developmental experiences rather than a set of repetitive worksheets.
Ensure suitable materials, safe activities and ways for every child to participate are available.
How can teachers prevent a theme from becoming a collection of unrelated decorations?
State a few clear learning intentions and connect activities to shared questions or experiences.
Use children's observations and conversations to link stories, play, making and exploration.
Review what children are actually doing and understanding instead of judging the theme by wall displays alone.
Explain three useful roles for a teaching team during outdoor play.
One adult can supervise an active movement area and notice emerging risks.
Another can support a small exploration group while maintaining agreed sightlines and communication.
The team should coordinate transitions and attendance checks, changing responsibilities according to staffing and children's needs rather than assuming one adult sees everything.
How can a teacher use a family suggestion without letting one family control the programme?
Listen for the child's experience or need behind the suggestion.
Consider whether an adapted version supports the programme's goals and is accessible to other children.
Explain the decision respectfully and continue inviting a range of family views rather than giving priority according to influence or resources.
Suggest three ways to organise reusable classroom materials responsibly.
Inspect and clean materials, rejecting items with sharp edges, unsafe residues or unsuitable small parts.
Sort and label them in accessible containers appropriate to children's use.
Regularly review condition and replace damaged items; reused materials are not automatically safe simply because they are inexpensive.
How can a daily plan accommodate different rest needs?
Provide a predictable quieter period and notice individual signs of tiredness.
Offer a comfortable supervised resting option alongside quiet activity where practical.
Discuss relevant routines with families and adapt sensitively rather than force every child to sleep or remain active for the same duration.
Why should planning record adaptations as well as the main activity?
Adaptations make support for language, mobility, sensory or communication needs explicit.
They help different adults offer consistent opportunities rather than improvise only after exclusion occurs.
Reviewing them shows which arrangements improved participation and what still needs adjustment.
A preschool timetable contains mostly worksheets and assembly. Suggest a balanced redesign.
Replace long seated blocks with opportunities for indoor and outdoor play, movement, conversation and creative exploration.
Retain predictable routines for arrival, meals, hygiene and rest, using them as caring learning experiences.
Offer a mix of child choice, small-group guidance and brief whole-group experiences, with accessible materials and language support.
Observe engagement and development, then adjust the schedule; balance depends on children's needs and meaningful participation, not equal minutes for every activity.
Explain how to prepare a safe and inclusive pretend-market corner.
Choose large, safe pretend goods and accessible containers, checking materials for damage and unsuitable small parts.
Provide pictures, familiar words and varied roles so children can participate through speech, gesture, sorting or exchanging objects.
Model respectful interaction and rotate opportunities without assigning buying, selling or carrying by gender or perceived ability.
Observe counting, language and cooperation in play, extending ideas through questions while avoiding formal written calculations beyond children's readiness.
How would you involve families in a classroom theme about local food without creating expense or competition?
Invite voluntary stories, names, pictures or descriptions of familiar foods, accepting spoken contributions in home languages.
Make clear that purchases and elaborate prepared displays are unnecessary and that the centre will provide essential materials.
Represent dietary and cultural diversity respectfully; check allergies and safety before any tasting activity.
Use contributions in conversation and pretend play, and share children's learning without comparing families' spending or treating one food tradition as superior.
Describe a practical process for improving a crowded classroom layout.
Observe where congestion, collisions or exclusion occur during actual routines and play.
Remove unnecessary obstacles and define accessible activity areas while keeping exits, supervision and movement routes clear.
Distribute popular materials and use suitable group arrangements to reduce crowding without denying children choice.
Try the revised layout, gather children's and colleagues' feedback, and review whether participation and safety improved; do not assume attractive furniture placement alone solves the problem.
Explain how to respond when a planned activity is too difficult for most children.
Stop interpreting difficulty as disobedience and observe which steps, materials or language create barriers.
Simplify the task, demonstrate a manageable part or offer more accessible materials while retaining its meaningful purpose.
Allow children different ways to participate and provide guidance without completing the whole product for them.
Record what the experience revealed and revise future planning, using development and interest rather than pressure to finish the original plan as the measure of success.
Design an inclusive arrival routine for an ECCE centre.
Arrange a welcoming supervised entry where each child is acknowledged by name and the responsible adult can exchange essential information privately.
Provide simple accessible places for belongings and a visual cue for the next activity, helping children who need support rather than expecting immediate independence.
Offer a small choice of familiar settling activities, such as looking at books, construction or drawing, so arrival does not require everyone to perform publicly.
Respond calmly to separation distress and agree supportive steps with the family, recognising that adjustment varies between children.

Check attendance and relevant health or care information, then guide a predictable transition into the programme. Review whether the routine supports safety, belonging and participation rather than merely fast entry.
Explain how a teacher can turn an unexpected interest in insects into a coherent short project.
Listen to children's questions and observe what interests them, distinguishing curiosity from fear and avoiding forced contact with insects.
Plan safe observation of local insects without handling unknown species or damaging habitats, using pictures when direct observation is unsuitable.
Connect experiences through drawing, movement, storytelling, counting visible features and comparing observations, keeping tasks developmentally appropriate.
Document children's ideas and revisit them through conversation, allowing the project to change as new questions arise instead of enforcing a fixed decorative outcome.

Conclude with a shared display or retelling that represents different contributions, then reflect on learning and participation. The teacher supplies accurate support while preserving inquiry and respect for living things.
Propose a response when outdoor space is limited but children need daily movement.
Assess the available space and identify hazards, safe boundaries and accessibility needs before selecting activities.
Use small supervised groups and staggered opportunities so children can move without overcrowding; coordinate adults' responsibilities and transitions.
Offer varied movement experiences such as balancing on floor markings, stretching, action songs and safe obstacle routes suited to the space and children's abilities.
Plan indoor alternatives for unsuitable weather while continuing to seek feasible safe outdoor opportunities through appropriate centre arrangements.

Observe participation, fatigue and enjoyment and revise the plan accordingly. Limited space calls for thoughtful organisation, not the removal of movement or risky use of public areas without safeguards.
Explain how to organise a community walk as an early learning experience.
Select a nearby accessible destination with a clear learning purpose, such as noticing community services, and assess the route, weather and potential hazards.
Follow the centre's required consent, staffing and safeguarding procedures, plan communication and emergency arrangements, and check individual support needs.
Prepare children through conversation and simple expectations, using familiar languages and visual cues without frightening them.
During the walk, maintain supervision and attendance checks while allowing safe observation and questions rather than rushing through a list of facts.
After returning, use drawings, role play or shared storytelling to revisit experiences and record what children noticed. Evaluate both participation and safety before planning another visit.
Describe a planning cycle that uses observation without turning preschool into constant testing.
Begin with developmental aims, knowledge of the children and their interests, then select accessible play and routine experiences that offer meaningful learning opportunities.
Prepare materials, space, timing and adaptations, identifying a few aspects of participation or learning to notice rather than a checklist for every moment.
Observe unobtrusively during activity, supporting children when needed and allowing spontaneous ideas to influence the experience.
Review brief records and children's contributions with the teaching team to identify strengths, barriers and useful next steps, avoiding rankings or fixed labels.
Revise subsequent plans and communicate relevant insights with families. Observation should improve the programme while protecting time for relationships, play and exploration.

pyqs.question: What is balanced curriculum?
answer: A balanced curriculum is one in which all five developmental domains are represented — language, physical, cognitive, socio-emotional and aesthetic-creativity — preferably within the same activity, with nothing taught formally or ahead of what the child can do.

pyqs.question: Write three principles in planning ECCE programme.
answer: Any three of the six planning principles will carry the answer. These are the ones I would write.

1. Developmentally appropriate. The activity must be one a child of that age can actually do, with the materials the centre really has, without an adult helping at every step. The test: can a child do it without an adult's hand on it?

2. Play- and activity-based. The plan is written as experiences and activities, not as lessons with outcomes attached, and the timetable actively protects time for them. A programme that is 80 per cent teacher-led is a primary programme in a small room, and the useful question is whether the plan would still run if the board and the textbook disappeared.

3. Child-centred and inclusive. Children take part in choosing and in evaluating, and nothing assumes a single home language, a single family structure, a physically average body or a particular amount of adult help at home. Would the activity work for a child who speaks only Mising, or for a child who cannot walk?

pyqs.question: What is theme-based activity? Prepare a weekly plan by taking a single theme for holistic development of a child of early childhood.
answer: A theme-based activity is one built around a broad subject — flowers, vegetables, birds, water, family, transport, community helpers or animals — that children explore from several directions across all five domains. A theme holds many activities and spans the whole week; an activity is one event inside it. The essence of the approach is integrated learning and learning by doing: the child meets the same idea through the hand, the eye, the ear and the mouth, and the concept forms out of the experience rather than out of an explanation.
Weekly plan — Theme: Water (class: 3–6 years, 25 children, one teacher with one helper)
Concepts carried by the theme: water comes in many forms; the same amount fits in different shapes; living things need water; water is shared, so we take turns.

Monday — Bringing water in. Real matkas, bottles, a bucket and a mug are placed out and the children simply play. Later the teacher asks, which one holds more? We watch who pours and who only watches. Domains: cognitive, physical, language. Materials: household containers, a bucket.

Tuesday — Carrying and building. Two children carry a bucket each from the tank to the plants; a relay with water pots; a block bridge over a water tray. Domains: physical (balance, bilateral coordination, endurance), cognitive (spatial planning), socio-emotional (turns, shared task). Materials: buckets, pots, blocks.

Wednesday — Words and story. Collect words for water in the home language; name the parts of a tap and a matka; the story of the thirsty crow, retold over two days; a rhyme with actions. Domains: language, socio-emotional. Materials: none beyond voice, and a few picture cards.

Thursday — Making and noticing. Floating and sinking with a stick, a leaf and a stone; finding where the tray leaks and mending it with cloth; painting the reflection on the surface; block-printing a ripple pattern. Domains: cognitive, aesthetic and creativity, physical. Materials: clay, cloth, washable colour, blocks.

Friday — Care and sharing. Why is the queue at the tap long? Taking turns to fill the school's pots; watering the shade corner; a circle song using every child's name. Domains: socio-emotional, language, aesthetic. Materials: song, plants.
Throughout the week, a wet-weather plan: the same water play indoors in trays, since in Assam rain cannot be scheduled out of a plan.

What we record while it runs: dated notes of who sorts, who persists, who waits, who speaks — the raw material of the Holistic Progress Card. And the test of the plan is simple: a child who joined on Thursday must still find something here to do.

pyqs.question: Write differences between project method of learning and theme-based method of learning.
answer:
- Organisation. In the project method one group works on a single self-chosen piece of work with an end product. In the theme-based method the teacher fixes a broad theme and many children explore it in different ways; there is no single end product.
- Who decides. The project is chosen by the children themselves; the theme is chosen by the teacher from what the children are already asking about.
- Outcome. A project ends in something made and presented; a theme ends in concrete experiences, new concepts and records across all five domains.

pyqs.question: What is curriculum? Mention the principles of constructing a balanced and contextualized curriculum for ECCE. Write a note on any one of them.
answer: Curriculum is the whole range of experiences a child is offered — what is planned, what the environment offers, what the adults say and do, what the children bring from home and community, and what the materials invite them to do. It is not the syllabus and not the textbook. In ECCE the textbook is usually absent by design, because nothing at this age is taught to a standard, nothing runs to a fixed period and nothing is completed.
The principles for constructing a balanced and contextualised ECCE curriculum are the six planning principles, and each is a corrective to a familiar failure.

1. Developmentally appropriate. The activity must be one a child of that age can actually do, with the materials actually available, without an adult hand on it. Writing before a child can hold a crayon well is not enrichment; it is practice at failure.
2. Holistic. Every area of development is represented, and preferably in the same activity rather than in separate periods. A child watering a plant is at once physical, cognitive, language, socio-emotional and aesthetic.
3. Contextualised. The curriculum grows out of what these children have — their language, the crops of the season, the work of their parents, the festivals on the local calendar, the water and sanitation conditions of the village.
4. Play- and activity-based. Written as experiences, not as lessons, with the timetable protecting time for them.
5. Child-centred and inclusive. Children participate in choosing and in evaluating; nothing assumes a single home language, a single family structure, an average body or a particular amount of adult help at home.
6. Flexible and cyclical. The plan is a hypothesis. The teacher observes, notes what the children actually did, and adjusts the next week — planning and assessment are the same loop seen from two ends.

Balance also carries a second meaning that examiners expect: balance across the six curricular issues the syllabus names — multilingualism, inclusion, gender, equality, the adverse effects of early formal instruction, and school readiness. A curriculum can cover all five domains beautifully and still be unbalanced in the sense that matters, if it runs entirely in one language, sorts materials by gender, or leaves the child who cannot walk standing at the edge.
A note on one principle in detail: contextualisation.

Take a rural Assamese pre-primary centre and the theme water. Contextualisation means concept and material both come from the children's own world. They carry buckets from the school tank, because that is the work they watch at home; the word for the container is the word their mother uses, not the word in the textbook; the story is about a queue at a tap, which is a queue they have stood in. Concept formation then happens without a lesson: which vessel holds more, why is one pot heavier than another of the same size, where is the leak, what will happen if we cover it. The concepts are conserved volume, capacity and cause and effect — genuine cognitive structures — but they were arrived at through material the children own.

The practical test takes one minute. Name three things in this activity a child here already knows. An activity built on a dhaki, a hu, or the paddy-seed count the parents bring home at harvest will pass. One built on a shape-sorting set from a catalogue will not, and the children will say so within ten minutes.

So I would put it this way. The curriculum of the early years is not what we decide children must learn, but the environment, the material, the conversation and the day we build around them — and it must be their own, or it will not take.

pyqs.question: Mention a few programmes that can be undertaken in school for establishing healthy home–school linkage.
answer: A linkage programme is a set of regular, scheduled activities, not an occasional meeting. The forms below are the ones the syllabus names, and they are worth running in this order, because each makes the next easier.

- Home visits, with an interpreter when the home language is not the school's. This is the only activity that gives the true picture of the child's language, care, nutrition and interests, and it brings back information the school badly needs.
- Open days and visiting hours. Parents come into the room and watch the ordinary day, not a performance arranged for them. This corrects the widespread belief that a good pre-primary class teaches letters and numbers, and it is where the teacher's own practice gets corrected too.
- Parent meetings and a parent council. Regular meetings on health, growth, nutrition and what the children are actually learning. The council advises the centre and, more usefully, carries messages back to families who never attend meetings.
- Take-home materials in the home language: a story to retell, a game to play with stones, a song. This keeps the learning going at home and quietly makes the child the family's teacher.
- Homework done together — talking about the day, reading any book that exists at home, visiting a market, doing a small household task side by side. Family time is the vehicle, and it is the form that reaches the poorest household, because it costs nothing.
- A weekly or fortnightly din's diary in the family's own language, with no written part: a picture of what the child made, the sentence the child spoke, and one question the parent answers. Short enough to be filled, which is why it is read.
- Using the community as a resource — the Anganwadi, the panchayat, the health centre, the library, local artisans and folk singers as guests in the room, and convergence meetings that put the Anganwadi and the pre-primary section in the same conversation.
One caution closes this: never enlist parents as unpaid helpers for cleaning duties. The moment a parent is treated as labour, the relationship is over.

pyqs.question: Briefly write about the need of theme-based activities in ECCE.
answer: A theme is a subject broad enough for children to explore from several directions and narrow enough to hold their attention. The syllabus is explicit that activities in ECCE be planned on a theme, cover all five domains, and use integrated learning and learning by doing. The official themes are flowers, vegetables, birds, water, family, transport, community helpers and animals.
The need is threefold.

- It gives the day a spine. A four-year-old cannot be given forty unrelated things, and a teacher who plans isolated activities ends up with nothing running. A theme holds them together, so a child joining on the second day still gets something to do. A theme that makes sense only to the planner is an activity, not a theme.
- It integrates the domains. On the theme water, one child carries two buckets from the tank (physical), asks which container holds more (cognitive), waits his turn at the tap (socio-emotional), names the parts of a matka (language), and block-prints a ripple pattern (aesthetic-creativity) — in the same hour, not five periods.
- It begins with concrete experience, which is what learning by doing means.

pyqs.question: Why is home–school linkage necessary in ECCE? For effective home–school linkage, what different activities would you carry out? Discuss.
answer: At this age the parents are the first educators, and a programme that treats them as visitors has misunderstood the stage. Four reasons make the linkage necessary.

- Continuity. What is learned at the centre has to survive at home, and what happens at home has to be understood at the centre. Neither half can do it alone.
- Language. Parents are the source of the child's home language, and a programme that does not know what language a child speaks at home cannot plan for the transition to school.
- Health and nutrition. Attendance, immunisation, sleep and feeding are school problems before they are health problems. The Anganwadi can weigh a child; only the family can change what she eats.
- Trust. A parent who has seen the room and spoken to the teacher will believe the teacher.

The activities that make it real:
- Home visits, with an interpreter or community worker where the home language is not the school's. Nothing else gives the true picture of the child's language, care, nutrition and interests.
- An open day and visiting hours, where parents watch the ordinary day rather than a performance. This also corrects the common belief that a good pre-primary class teaches letters.
- Parent meetings and a parent council — regular meetings on health, growth and development, and a council that can carry messages back to families who never attend.
- Take-home materials: simple, low-cost activities in the home language, requiring nothing the family must buy.
- Homework done together — talking about the day, reading any book at all, visiting a market, doing a small household task side by side. This reaches the poorest home, because it costs nothing.
- Local people as guests: a potter, a boatman, a weaver, a grandmother, sitting in the room talking about the work.
One caution: involve parents as partners with knowledge, never as unpaid helpers assigned cleaning duties. The moment a parent is treated as labour, the relationship is over.

pyqs.question: Write any two principles of a balanced curriculum on ECCE.
answer:
- Developmentally appropriate: the activity is one a child of that age can actually do, with the materials actually available, without an adult's hand on it at every step.
- Holistic: every domain is represented, and preferably inside the same activity rather than in separate periods.

pyqs.question: What is meant by long-term and short-term programme planning in regard to ECCE? Explain with appropriate examples.
answer: At this stage nothing is completed, so planning describes a range of experience and a rhythm rather than a sequence of lessons with outcomes attached. Planning happens at two horizons, and the two must agree with each other.

Long-term planning is the wider frame: the annual or term-wise programme, built around the children's age group, the local season, the agricultural calendar and the festivals on the local calendar. It answers the question, what should this group of children have experienced by the end of the year? An annual plan for a pre-primary section in an Assamese village might put the monsoon and paddy in September, the harvest and the post-harvest folk songs in November and December, Bihu and the seasonal foods in January, the new seedlings in March, with a block on water, sanitation and hygiene running through all of it. It also allocates the practical things: the term's themes, the visits, the parent meetings, the growth-monitoring schedule and the material budget.

Short-term planning is the daily and weekly working plan — what we will actually do in this room tomorrow. A weekly plan on the theme of water might spread across five days: Monday bringing real water containers and asking which holds more; Tuesday carrying two buckets from the tank; Wednesday the story of the thirsty crow and words for water in the home language; Thursday painting the reflection and block-printing a ripple; Friday talking about why the queue at the tap is long. Each day also fixes the daily rhythm: arrival and free play, circle time, snack, outdoor activity, rest, group activity, story and song, departure.

The two are joined by the principle of flexible and cyclical planning. A plan is a hypothesis, not a promise. If the children spent four days chasing a scooter in the yard, the week is re-sequenced around outdoor games. If the group sorts bottle caps by size without being asked, the next plan pushes seriation further. The long-term plan sets the direction, the short-term plan sets the road, and what the teacher observes while driving changes both. A term plan that observation cannot alter is not a plan; it is a schedule that has been mistaken for one.

pyqs.question: Write the principles of preparing a balanced and contextualized programme of Early Childhood Care and Education (ECCE).
answer: Planning an ECCE programme is not the same work as planning a primary programme, and six principles do most of the job. This is the list an examiner is looking for.

1. Developmentally appropriate. The activity must be one a child of that age can actually do, with the materials actually available, without an adult hand on it. Writing before a child can hold a crayon well is not enrichment; it is practice at failure.
2. Holistic. Every area of development is represented, preferably in the same activity rather than in separate periods. The test: point to the physical, cognitive, language, socio-emotional and aesthetic strand of this one activity.
3. Contextualised. The plan grows out of what the children in this centre have — their language, the crops of the season, the work of their parents, the festivals on the local calendar, the water and sanitation conditions of the village. The test: name three things in this plan a child here already knows. An activity built on a dhaki or a hu will pass; one built on a shape-sorting set from a catalogue will not, and the children will say so within ten minutes.
4. Play- and activity-based. The plan is written as experiences, not as lessons, and the timetable protects time for them. The test: could this run if the board and the textbook disappeared?
5. Child-centred and inclusive. Children participate in choosing and in evaluating; nothing assumes a single home language, a single family structure, an average body or a particular amount of adult help at home.
6. Flexible and cyclical. The teacher observes, notes what the children actually did, and adjusts the next week's plan. Planning and assessment are the same loop seen from two ends.

Balanced and contextualised, then, are not two separate virtues. A balanced programme covers all five domains; contextualised means the balance is drawn from the children in front of you, not from a textbook written three thousand kilometres away.

pyqs.question: Mention one theme-based activity for ensuring holistic development during ECCE.
answer: Under the theme Water: carrying two buckets from the tank to the garden. Physical (balance, grip, endurance), cognitive (which container holds more), language (naming the parts of a matka), socio-emotional (taking turns at the tap) and aesthetic (arranging the vessels by size).

pyqs.question: Discuss why proper management of classrooms, both inside and outside, is an important factor in ECCE.
answer: At this age management is not discipline in the ordinary sense. A three-year-old cannot be reasoned with, cannot be made to sit still because a lesson demands it, and does not understand punishment. What we manage is not the child's behaviour but the conditions under which it changes.

Inside, arrange the room so that movement is the default: low shelves, reachable material, floor space, a book corner, a sand-and-water corner, display at child height. Keep materials few, mixed and open-ended. The flow of the day matters more than its content — arrival, free play, circle, snack, outdoor time, rest, group activity, story, departure — because a predictable rhythm lowers friction better than any rule. Work in groups of four to six and rotate them; whole-class instruction does not belong below six.

Outside, zone the space for active play, quiet play, sand and water, climbing and a garden bed, and keep it safe but not sterile. Adults stand where they can see the whole space, and the ratio is about one adult to ten children. Change the conditions before you change the child.

pyqs.question: Write a short note on: Importance of parental and community involvement in ECCE.
answer: Importance of parental and community involvement in ECCE

It decides what the programme can actually do. What is learned at the centre has to survive at home, and parents are the source of the child's home language, so without knowing the family we cannot even plan the transition to school. Attendance, immunisation, sleep and feeding are school problems before they are health problems. And trust matters: a parent who has seen the room and spoken to the teacher will believe the teacher, where one handed only a diary will not. The community adds what no budget can buy — the potter's hands, a field, a folk song, the health centre.

pyqs.question: Mention one characteristic of theme-based activities.
answer: A theme is never a single lesson. One broad theme is explored through many activities that together reach all five domains — language, physical, cognitive, socio-emotional and aesthetic-creativity — each beginning with a concrete experience.

pyqs.question: Why is parental involvement important in ECCE?
answer: Because the family is the child's first school. Parents give the earliest language, the food, the affection and the habits of self-care, and whatever is learned at the centre has to survive at home — so parents must be partners, not visitors.

pyqs.question: Write two strategies for outside management of ECCE classroom.
answer: Outdoor space is not the leftover, so I would manage it on two lines.

- Zoning. Mark out separate areas for active play, quiet play, sand and water, a climbing or swinging structure and a garden bed, using plants, edges or low fencing rather than instructions to the children.
- Supervision without hovering. Position adults so that the whole space is visible, keep about one adult to ten children, and let the ground stay slightly risky — safe means a sound fence and a covered well, not a sterile concrete yard.

pyqs.question: Write about the necessities for planning and design of theme-based activities for ECCE.
answer: A theme is a subject broad enough for children to explore from several directions and narrow enough to hold their attention. Planning a theme is a five-step job, and the order matters.

1. Find the thread. Start from the children, not from the textbook. Ask what they have noticed recently — the rain, the buffaloes in the field, the new shop on the road — and choose the theme they are already asking about. A theme imported from a book is a theme that will not run.
2. Set the concepts. List the three or four big ideas the theme can carry, stated as concepts and not as activities. For flowers: living things need water and light; plants can be sorted and grouped; the same word can be a name, a colour and a shape. Concepts, not tasks.
3. Plan the concrete experiences first, before writing anything down. What will children actually do, see, handle and say? A seed soaked in a plate, a leaf rubbed and pressed, a rhyme sung, a story told, a visit to a garden. Concrete experience is the foundation; everything else is built on it.
4. Spread the activities across all five domains — language, physical, cognitive, socio-emotional and aesthetic-creativity — preferably in the same activity rather than in five separate periods.
5. Sequence, and decide in advance what you will record. Seeing comes before naming, naming before comparing, comparing before classifying. That record is what the Holistic Progress Card will later be made of.
Materials go with this: low-cost, locally available, safe, non-toxic and age-appropriate — nothing small enough to swallow, nothing sharp, no water without an adult present.

practice: What is an anecdotal record?
A brief dated factual account of a significant observed event or behaviour in its context.
What is a child portfolio?
A purposeful collection of a child's work and observation records showing learning and development over time.
What is an assessment indicator?
An observable sign used to consider a particular aspect of learning or development.
What is confidentiality in progress reporting?
Sharing a child's personal information only with people who appropriately need it and protecting it from unnecessary disclosure.
Why should an observation record include a date?
The date places the observation in time and helps track change across repeated observations.
What is an attendance register used for?
Recording which children attend and identifying patterns that may require supportive follow-up.
What is a strength-based comment?
A comment that recognises what a child can do and uses that understanding to identify constructive next steps.
What is meant by assessment evidence?
Information from observations, conversations or children's work that supports a judgement about learning or development.
What is a follow-up observation?
A later observation used to check progress or clarify an earlier impression in a relevant context.
What is a centre self-review?
A systematic examination of the centre's practices and conditions to identify strengths and improvements needed.
Distinguish an observation from an interpretation.
An observation records what was seen or heard, such as a child offering a block to a peer.
An interpretation proposes what it may mean, such as growing cooperation, and should be checked against further evidence.
Why is one difficult day insufficient for a developmental judgement?
Illness, tiredness, unfamiliar surroundings or distress can affect performance on a particular day.
Repeated observations across suitable contexts give a fairer picture of the child's abilities and support needs.
Suggest two safeguards when storing digital progress records.
Restrict access to authorised people and protect devices or accounts appropriately.
Collect and share only necessary information, following the centre's consent and retention arrangements.
Why should a portfolio include work from different dates?
It allows teachers and families to notice change and developing strategies over time.
It prevents a single polished product from being mistaken for a complete picture of learning.
Give two reasons to record the context of a child's response.
The materials, language and level of adult help affect what the response demonstrates.
Context helps another educator interpret the evidence fairly and plan suitable follow-up.
How can a teacher seek a young child's view of their own work?
Invite the child to describe or show what they tried and what they liked, accepting gestures or home-language responses.
Record the child's meaning without replacing it with an adult judgement of whether the product looks correct.
Why should attendance concerns be discussed supportively with families?
Absence may reflect health, transport, care or other practical difficulties rather than indifference.
A respectful conversation helps identify feasible support without blaming or publicly exposing the family.
What is the difference between a developmental concern and a diagnosis?
A concern is an observation that suggests further attention or support may be needed.
A diagnosis requires an appropriately qualified assessment; a teacher should not assign it from classroom impressions alone.
Why should assessment tools be accessible in the child's familiar language?
A language barrier can hide understanding and make a task appear harder than the underlying concept.
Accessible communication helps distinguish the learning being assessed from proficiency in an unfamiliar language.
How can a checklist be used without reducing a child to ticks?
Record relevant examples and context alongside indicators, including support provided.
Combine the checklist with other observations and use it to plan learning rather than rank children.
Rewrite the label 'lazy child' as an evidence-based observation and next step.
Record an observable event: 'During today's block activity, the child watched for five minutes and joined after an invitation.'
Consider possible influences such as unfamiliar materials, tiredness or uncertainty instead of assuming a character flaw.
Offer a familiar entry point and observe participation again before drawing broader conclusions.
How can a teacher assess cooperation during shared play?
Notice specific actions such as sharing materials, negotiating roles or responding to a peer's request.
Record the context and adult support, observing on more than one occasion and in different groups.
Use the evidence to plan suitable modelling or supported play, rather than label a quiet child uncooperative.
Suggest three ways to make a progress discussion understandable to families.
Use clear everyday language and the family's preferred accessible communication method.
Share a few concrete examples of strengths and developing skills instead of unexplained scores or jargon.
Agree on feasible next steps and invite the family's observations, checking that the discussion is understood.
How should a teacher handle conflicting observations from home and the centre?
Listen respectfully and record the different contexts in which the behaviour occurs.
Consider differences in language, familiarity, support and expectations rather than decide immediately that one account is wrong.
Plan further observations and supportive opportunities, then review the combined evidence with the family.
What should be included in a useful work-sample annotation?
Record the date, activity and relevant learning focus.
Describe what the child did or explained, including any help received.
Note a tentative interpretation and a suitable next opportunity, keeping the original work's meaning distinct from adult assumptions.
How can records help a child move to a new classroom?
Provide a concise account of strengths, interests and helpful participation supports.
Share necessary care or developmental information securely with appropriate staff and family involvement.
Use the information to support continuity while allowing the new teacher to form fresh observations rather than inherit fixed labels.
Why can public ranking harm the purpose of ECCE assessment?
It encourages comparison between children rather than attention to each child's learning and support needs.
It can stigmatise children whose development, language or circumstances differ and narrow learning to visible performance.
Private descriptive feedback is more useful for planning experiences and building confidence.
Suggest three checks before using a commercially available preschool assessment sheet.
Check whether its tasks and indicators match the children's developmental stage and the intended learning focus.
Check language, cultural relevance and accessibility so the sheet does not measure avoidable barriers.
Check whether results can support teaching alongside other evidence rather than produce unsupported diagnoses or rankings.
How can a centre assess the quality of adult-child interaction?
Observe whether adults listen, respond warmly and allow children time to communicate.
Notice whether guidance is respectful and inclusive, especially during distress, conflict and routines.
Use examples for team reflection and improvement, protecting privacy and avoiding a review based only on staged demonstrations.
Explain how health and attendance records can inform programme support.
Patterns may indicate that a child is missing experiences or needs adjustments after illness.
Teachers can discuss relevant concerns privately with families and coordinate appropriate support through established services.
Records guide care and access; they should not be used to blame families or make medical conclusions beyond the teacher's competence.
A child rarely speaks in whole-group discussion. Explain a fair assessment response.
Observe communication in small groups, play and familiar routines, accepting gesture, home language and other forms of expression.
Check whether the setting, language demands or turn-taking arrangements limit participation before inferring a lack of understanding.
Provide predictable, low-pressure opportunities and record specific responses over time, including the support offered.
Discuss observations sensitively with the family and seek appropriate guidance if concerns persist, without forcing public speech or assigning a diagnosis from silence alone.
Describe how to select a balanced set of evidence for a progress report.
Start from relevant developmental and learning areas rather than collect only handwriting or counting products.
Choose dated observations, conversations and work samples from different activities that show strengths and emerging skills.
Include context, accessibility adjustments and adult help so the evidence is interpreted fairly.
Use the selection to write clear descriptive comments and practical next steps, avoiding excessive documentation or claims unsupported by the samples.
How should a teacher correct an inaccurate progress record?
Check the original observation and discuss the discrepancy with relevant staff rather than quietly changing an uncertain judgement into a new certainty.
Correct the record through the centre's appropriate process, preserving a clear account of what was amended when necessary.
Explain the correction privately to the family or authorised recipients if the inaccurate information was shared.
Review the cause, such as unclear wording or a mistaken identity, and improve recording practices to prevent recurrence.
Explain how a centre can use an interaction-quality concern to plan improvement.
Describe the concern with specific examples, such as adults repeatedly interrupting children's explanations, rather than a vague judgement that staff are uncaring.
Discuss its effect on participation and agree on practical changes such as waiting time, attentive listening and respectful guidance.
Provide modelling, peer support or training and make room for staff to reflect on difficult routines.
Observe again after the change and review evidence of improvement, treating quality development as an ongoing process rather than a one-time inspection score.
A portfolio contains only work completed with heavy adult help. What should the teacher change?
Label existing samples honestly with the type of assistance provided so they are not misread as independent performance.
Collect examples from ordinary play and routines where the child's own choices, strategies and responses are visible.
Include children's explanations and observations across time, allowing unfinished or imperfect work to show meaningful learning.
Use the portfolio to plan support and communicate progress rather than select only polished products for display.
Explain how to assess an inclusive small-group sorting activity.
Clarify the learning focus, such as noticing similarities and differences, so assessment does not accidentally depend on handwriting or fluency in an unfamiliar language.
Offer safe accessible objects and allow children to point, move, describe or otherwise communicate their grouping decisions, adapting physical access as needed.
Observe strategies and explanations during play, noting the prompts or help provided rather than recording only whether the final arrangement matches an adult example.
Gather evidence across occasions and consider alternative sensible groupings, such as colour or shape, before treating a response as an error.
Use findings to offer a suitable next challenge or support and share concrete progress with families. The purpose is to improve learning opportunities, not rank the group.
Describe a responsible response to repeated observations suggesting a child needs additional developmental support.
Record specific dated observations across relevant contexts, including strengths and the adaptations already tried, without attaching a diagnostic label.
Check possible barriers such as unfamiliar language, inaccessible materials or limited opportunities and provide suitable classroom support promptly.
Discuss the pattern privately and respectfully with the family, listening to their observations and explaining the concern in clear, non-alarming language.
Follow the centre's referral arrangements to appropriate qualified services when needed, with family involvement and confidentiality; do not promise a diagnosis or outcome.

Continue inclusive participation and review support using further evidence and professional guidance. A referral should expand access to help, not justify excluding the child from ordinary experiences.
Plan a manageable documentation system for a busy ECCE teacher.
Identify essential records for attendance, care, learning and communication, distinguishing required information from attractive but unnecessary paperwork.
Use brief dated observation notes with clear child identification and context, focusing on a few children or learning areas at a time while remaining responsive to significant events.
Organise selected work samples and notes securely so change over time can be reviewed without retaining every product or duplicating the same information repeatedly.
Set a regular short review time to turn evidence into planning decisions and concise family feedback, sharing responsibilities appropriately within the team.
Periodically assess whether documentation improves care and teaching while protecting time for interaction. A manageable system values useful evidence over the volume of files produced.
Explain how to conduct a constructive family conference about a child's progress.
Prepare a small selection of concrete examples showing interests, strengths and developing skills, ensuring the information is accurate and relevant to the child.
Arrange a private accessible conversation at a feasible time and begin by inviting the family's perspective rather than presenting a one-way verdict.
Describe observations in clear language, distinguish evidence from interpretation and avoid comparisons with classmates or unsupported labels.
Agree on a few realistic next steps for the centre and home, using ordinary routines and materials rather than expensive tasks or pressure for formal performance.
Record the agreement securely and plan a follow-up to review progress. The conference should strengthen shared understanding and support, including when concerns need further professional advice.
Describe a centre improvement cycle focused on children's experience rather than appearance alone.
Review ordinary daily practice using observations, records and input from staff and families, including how children experience safety, care, play and inclusion.
Identify a specific priority with evidence, such as children waiting too long for materials or an inaccessible activity area, instead of judging quality only by colourful walls.
Agree on feasible actions, responsibilities and resources, connecting changes to the relevant quality standard and children's needs.
Implement the changes with staff support and observe whether participation, relationships or learning opportunities improve in everyday situations.
Document the results and remaining barriers, then revise the plan. Continuous review should build a better experience for all children rather than prepare a temporary display for visitors.

pyqs.question: Define assessment. How is ECCE assessment different from other learning levels? Explain with example.
answer: Assessment means judging the extent to which learning has taken place. That definition is too thin for the early years, and the difference matters.

Testing measures a child against a standard, in a situation someone designed, and produces a number. Assessment observes what a child can already do, in ordinary activity, and produces a description. At every level the distinction exists, but below six it becomes a matter of principle, because a test administered to a four-year-old measures the examiner more than the child: a strange adult, a strange room, questions with no material in the hands, and a demand to produce an answer on demand rather than in play.

So ECCE assessment differs in these ways.
- It is continuous, not periodic. It happens while children are playing and costs nothing extra. A test week in an ECCE centre is a lost week.
- It is based only on observation. The evidence is what the child does with a real material, over real time, with real people around.
- It is embedded in play, so the activity assessed is the activity the children believe they are playing in.
- It covers all five domains and gives no single label.
- It is measured against the child's own previous level, not against the class.
- It is qualitative, not competitive. No marks out of ten, no ranking on a wall.
- It is never used for selection, labelling or admission.

An example. In a Grade 3 classroom the teacher gives a unit test, marks it out of twenty, and finds that twenty-eight children can subtract within a hundred. In a pre-primary class the teacher watches four children fit ten bottle caps from largest to smallest, and sees that three manage it unaided and can then re-sort by colour, while the fourth still confuses size with number. That observation is worth more than any test: it is dated, repeatable, names the actual difficulty, and tells the teacher exactly what to do next — more guided play with the same material, not a worksheet.

pyqs.question: Prepare a progress report proforma for pre-school children.
answer: The progress report turns a teacher's records into something a family can use. A record kept in the register helps the teacher; a report reaches the home and changes what the family does. A good proforma therefore leaves a place for the parent's own comment as well as the teacher's.
Sample proforma — Pre-school Progress Report

Part A. Identification
Name of child ____ ; date of birth ____ ; admission date ____ ; class/age ____ ; parent or guardian ____ ; address and contact ____ ; attendance this term ____.

Part B. Observation summary (dated behaviour, not grades)
- Language — ____
- Physical — ____
- Cognitive — ____
- Socio-emotional — ____
- Aesthetic and creativity — ____
- Health and nutrition — ____
Part C. Present level in my words — What your child can now do: ____ (begin here, with a strength)
Part D. Change since last report — What she could not do in September and can do now: ____
Part E. One activity for home — ____ (something the family can do this week, in the home language)
Part F. Teacher's signature and date ____ ; Parent's comment and signature ____

Three rules govern the filling of it. Report what the child can do, not what she lacks, because a parent told only about failure will look for a remedy everywhere except where the remedy is. Use the child's own behaviour in concrete terms — she has started sharing is a report; she has improved in sharing is a judgment nobody can act on. And never compare one child with another, because that comparison belongs in the teacher's head, not on paper a family keeps for years.

pyqs.question: Mention one principle of assessment.
answer: Assessment is based on observation, and only on observation. The evidence is what a child does with a real material, over real time, with real people around — never what he merely says he can do.

pyqs.question: Write differences between authentic assessment and developmental assessment.
answer:
- What is watched. Authentic assessment watches the child doing real things in real activity — the leaf he sorts, the bridge he builds with blocks. Developmental assessment asks what the child can do now compared with what he could do earlier.
- The benchmark. Authentic assessment sets no standard beyond the ordinary demands of the activity. Developmental assessment uses the child's own previous level as the yardstick, never the class average.
- Together they answer the only question that matters here: what can this child do now that he could not do before?

pyqs.question: Prepare a sample progress report for a pre-school child.
answer: Here is a filled-in sample, so that the difference between a record and a judgement is visible.

Sample Progress Report
Child: Manju Das. Age: 4 years 4 months. Class: pre-primary. Period: September to December. Attendance: present 78 of 86 days; absent 8, of which 5 were with fever and followed up.

Language — Manju now uses four- and five-word sentences where in September she used single words. On 4 December she narrated the whole sequence of what happened at the pond without prompting. She answers in Mising at home and Assamese in class, and is beginning to join the Assamese rhyme for bathua-bhat.

Physical — She pedals the tricycle up the slope unaided and holds her crayon in a tripod grip. She buttons her own coat now. She was shy about the rough-and-tumble corner in September; on 14 November she was last to leave it.

Cognitive — She sorted ten bottle caps by size unaided and can then re-sort by colour when the rule changes. Attention has lengthened from about two minutes to about ten. She tried the pulley four times before asking for help, and then succeeded.

Socio-emotional — She joined the group game after ten minutes and stayed to the end, and coped with losing the race without crying. Separation at drop-off is still difficult on Mondays; on other days she walks in and greets the group.
Aesthetic and creativity — She chose colours deliberately and stayed with the block-printing to the end of the session. Her clay pot from the theme water was displayed at child height.
Health and nutrition — Weight 13.1 kg against 12.4 kg in September; height 100 cm. No referral needed.

One thing you can do at home: please keep talking with her in Mising at home about the stories we are reading here. She retells them to her grandmother in Mising, and that retelling is where the words are settling.
Teacher: (signature)  Parent: (signature)

Note what makes this a report and not a score. Every entry carries a date and a behaviour somebody else could also see, it begins with a strength, and it ends in an action the family can carry out. There is no comparison with the class anywhere in it.

pyqs.question: Explain why it is necessary to maintain progress records of children.
answer: Assessment in ECCE answers one question: what can this child do now that he could not do before? The record is the only place where that answer is written down, and without it the teacher is left with memory and impression.
The reasons records are necessary are these.

- They are the evidence assessment rests on. Assessment here is continuous, observation-based and play-based, and the evidence is what a child does with real material over real time. A useful entry carries a date and a behaviour — sorted ten bottle caps by size unaided. Words like good and average are not entries, because nobody can act on them.
- They change the programme. The Holistic Progress Card carries five dated columns, one for each domain, and the next plan is built on what the card shows is missing.
- They are the meeting point with the family. A register entry helps the teacher; a report reaches the home and changes what the family does. So reporting begins with a strength, describes behaviour rather than quality, covers all five domains, uses the parent's language, and never compares the child with others.
- They give continuity and protection. The admission, attendance and stock registers are official records, and attendance at this age is a health and nutrition indicator, not merely administration. They must never be used for selection or ranking.

pyqs.question: Write a short note on: Observation and evaluation in ECCE.
answer: Observation and evaluation in ECCE

Observation is deliberate watching during ordinary play: does she hold the crayon in a working grip, does he wait for his turn, can the group sort ten caps by size. The teacher records what the child actually did, with a date, and describes the behaviour rather than labelling the quality. Evaluation is the next step: what has moved since the last observation, which domain is still weak, and what the plan must therefore change. Planning and assessment are the same loop seen from two ends.

pyqs.question: Discuss 8 key standards to ensure quality Early Childhood Care and Education (ECCE).
answer: The syllabus names eight standards against which an ECCE programme is judged — and against which we should judge our own plan. They concern the environment, the process and the people.

1. Safe and secure environment. Sound fencing, a covered well, secured water points, safe furniture and material, a known emergency procedure, and the centre's address on record with the nearest health facility.
2. Health and nutrition. Check-up on admission, monthly growth monitoring, drinking water, sanitation, a midday meal, and absence followed up and referred.
3. Developmentally appropriate curriculum. Activities matched to the age; all five domains covered; nothing taught formally or ahead of the child's capacity.
4. Learning through play and activity. Long periods of free and guided play with materials the children reach themselves; the teacher extends the play rather than instructing.
5. Trained and adequate staff. Trained in ECCE, present in the room, not pulled away to other duties, with the adult–child ratio held at about one adult to ten children.
6. Family and community partnership. Parents known, visited and welcomed, their knowledge of the child recorded, and the community used as a resource.
7. Inclusive programme. Every child welcome regardless of disability, gender, language, caste, religion or income, with a space and material designed so that every child can actually take part.
8. Continuous assessment and improvement. Progress observed, entered on the Holistic Progress Card and used to change the programme, with the admission, attendance and stock registers complete.

Read together, the eight describe one thing: a programme that keeps the child safe, keeps the child fed, keeps the child playing, and pays attention to what the child can now do. A centre that satisfies standard 8 while failing standard 5 is only documenting bad practice.

pyqs.question: What is Holistic Progress Card (HPC)?
answer: The Holistic Progress Card is the official card maintained for every child in an ECCE programme. It carries dated notes of what the child actually did across all five developmental domains, and it describes behaviour rather than grades.

pyqs.question: Mention one key standard for ensuring quality ECCE.
answer: A safe and secure environment: the building, furniture and material are safe, the fence, the well and any water point are secured, staff know the emergency procedure, and the centre's address is on record with the nearest health facility.

pyqs.question: Mention any two tools of assessment in ECCE.
answer:
- Observation. The teacher watches systematically during ordinary play — does she hold the crayon in a working grip, does he wait for his turn — and records what the child actually did. It costs nothing extra, because it happens while the children are playing.
- The Holistic Progress Card. The official child-level record, carrying dated notes of behaviour across all five domains. It tells the teacher what to change in the programme and the parent what to do at home.

pyqs.question: Discuss the key principles of assessment in ECCE.
answer: Assessment at this stage has one job: to describe what a child can now do, so that the programme can be changed and the parent can be told something true. Seven principles follow from that job.

1. Continuous and part of the programme, not an event. It happens while the children are playing and costs nothing extra. A test week in an ECCE centre is a lost week.
2. Based on observation, and only on observation. The evidence is what a child does with a real material, over real time, with real people around — never what he says he can do.
3. Play-based and embedded, not separated from the children. The activity that is assessed is the activity they believe they are playing in.
4. Holistic. All five domains, no single label. A child is five things at once, and a report that says average without saying average in what is worse than no report.
5. Developmentally appropriate, and measured against the child's own previous level. At this age the gain over time is the finding.
6. Qualitative and descriptive, not quantitative and competitive. Words, examples and a description of behaviour — not a number out of ten, and never a ranking on a wall.
7. Used for support and programme improvement, never for selection or labelling. Records must never travel outside the centre as a verdict on a child.

Every one of these is a consequence of a single question: what can this child do now that he could not do before? If our answer to a child's progress is a mark out of twenty, we have stopped asking that question and started asking a different one, whose answer helps nobody.

pyqs.question: What is Holistic Progress Card (HPC)? Prepare a sample holistic progress report proforma for pre-school children.
answer: The Holistic Progress Card is the official child-level document of an ECCE programme. It is a card maintained for every child, recording dated evidence of progress across all five developmental domains — language, physical, cognitive, socio-emotional, and aesthetic-appreciation and creativity. It informs the programme and reports to the parent. It carries descriptions of what the child did, never scores. A child who cannot do anything on the day you test him is not a child who knows nothing; he is a child you did not watch.
Sample proforma:

1. Child identification — Name; date of birth; date of admission; centre enrolment number; parent/guardian name, address and contact.
2. Period covered — From ____ to ____ (Term I / Term II); class/age group ____.
3. Attendance during the period — Present ____ days; absent ____ days; reason and follow-up.
4. Domain-wise dated observation sheet:
- Language — vocabulary, sentence length, sequencing a story, listening to the end.
- Physical — gross motor, fine-motor grip, self-care and independence, participation in outdoor activity.
- Cognitive — attention span, matching, sorting, seriation, persistence.
- Socio-emotional — confidence, cooperation, separation from parent, tolerance of frustration.
- Aesthetic and creativity — expression, design, willingness to try, care taken with the work.
5. Health and nutrition note — growth measured, any referral made.
6. Teacher's overall remark for the term, beginning with a strength and ending with one action the family can carry out.

An entry is useful only if it carries a date and describes a behaviour somebody else could also see: '4 March — sorted ten bottle caps by size unaided; tried the pulley four times before asking for help.' Words like good, average and needs improvement are not entries; they cannot be acted on, and they tell the parent nothing she can do on Monday.
